title: Ancient DNA offers clues about mysterious prehistoric settlement in China
content:
In 2012, archaeologists started excavating a site called Shimao, located in the Yellow River valley in the northern part of China’s Shaanxi province. This massive and socially stratified settlement dates to the late Neolithic period — around 3,800–4,300 years ago. Writing in *Nature*, Chen *et al*.1 investigate the genomes of the people who inhabited this mysterious ancient city.

Read the paper: Ancient DNA from Shimao city records kinship practices in Neolithic China![](http://media.nature.com/w400/magazine-assets/d41586-025-03593-5/d41586-025-03593-5_51741082.jpg)


Many qualities of Shimao are perplexing. For one, the settlement is farther north than the Central Plains (Fig. 1), where other Neolithic Yellow River cultures such as the Yangshao (5000–3000 bc) and Longshan (2500–1800 bc) flourished and where Chinese civilizations later developed. The site is impressively large at around 4 square kilometres, and it has an unusual architectural style characterized by massive stone walls, which is different from the rammed-earth walls of settlements in the Central Plains. The substantial number of jade items, and other diverse artefacts, are indicative of extensive trade networks or long-distance connections2.

![Figure 1](http://media.nature.com/lw767/magazine-assets/d41586-025-03593-5/d41586-025-03593-5_51757950.jpg)

**Figure 1 | Origins of the people of Shimao.** Shimao is a late Neolithic settlement in northern China that has puzzled archaeologists because of its unusual architecture and diverse cultural artefacts. This massive walled city is located in the Yellow River valley, north of the Central Plains where early Chinese civilizations flourished. Chen *et al*.1 used ancient-DNA analysis to investigate the population history of Shimao. They found that the Shimao people originated from a local population that had inhabited the region hundreds of years earlier, and might have been related to the Yangshao culture of the Central Plains or other cultures from the Ordos region. The Shimao population is genetically similar to people from a settlement called Taosi, suggesting possible shared ancestry. The findings also suggested that there are minor genetic influences from the steppe regions to the north and from southern rice-farming cultures from the Yangtze River region (Qujialing and Shijiahe cultures).

Archaeologists are desperately seeking answers to questions that cultural artefacts alone have a limited capacity to answer. Chen and colleagues turned to analyses of ancient genomes from the individuals buried at the site and at surrounding settlements to address the origins of the Shimao people, their population history and their cultural practices, such as kinship patterns.

The authors started by reconstructing the genetic make-up of the people of Shimao and their predecessors (pre-Shimao populations). By comparing these genomic data to published ancient-DNA data from other populations in northern China, the authors found that the Shimao people mostly derived from a population that inhabited the local area about 300 years earlier. The pre-Shimao populations were closely tied, culturally and genetically, to the Yangshao population of the Central Plains. Cultural influences from the Ordos region (perhaps from the Haishengbulang culture) are also noticeable2. It seems that this hybrid local tradition continued without a substantial population shift until Shimao appeared hundreds of years later.

Women were at the centre of social networks in Iron Age Britain![](http://media.nature.com/w400/magazine-assets/d41586-025-03593-5/d41586-025-03593-5_51107818.jpg)


Shimao was also influenced by cultures from the steppe regions farther to the north, as evidenced by stone figurines, some bronze artefacts and the extensive use of sheep, goats and cattle instead of the pig-centred animal husbandry of the Central Plains2. However, the authors did not detect large genetic contributions from the north in the Shimao population as a whole. A few outlier individuals from Shimao and pre-Shimao populations are closely related to the northern steppe populations, suggesting that there was some cultural and genetic exchange between these groups, but no large-scale migrations.

Chen and colleagues also found minor genetic contributions to Shimao people from southern rice-producing populations, but this is not a complete surprise. Archaeological and genetic evidence3,4 has suggested that the Qujialing (3400–2500 bc) and Shijiahe (2500–2000 bc) Neolithic cultures in the middle reaches of Yangtze River (south of the Yellow River) expanded northwards starting from the late Yangshao period and continued to expand in the following Longshan period. The results of Chen and colleagues, and others4, imply that there were more southern genetic contributions in people from the Longshan culture in the Central Plains than in the people of Shimao, confirming the route of the Qujialing and Shijiahe expansions towards the Central Plains first and then farther north.

A striking feature of Shimao is the considerable number of human sacrifices that have been identified there: more than 80 human skulls were found buried at the city’s eastern gate. Such large numbers of human skulls have not appeared in any other archaeological sites in China until those dating to the early Shang period (about 1500–1300 bc). Although previous analyses of the skeletal remains suggested that most of the people sacrificed were female, Chen and colleagues’ ancient DNA evidence indicated that most skulls (nine of the ten analysed) were in fact from male individuals. However, until the discrepancy can be resolved with genomic analyses of more individuals, it is hard to make further interpretations about why these sacrifices were made.

Evidence of human sacrifices was also found in some burial sites of people from the elite class of Shimao. According to the authors’ genomic analysis, most of these individuals (20 out of 26) were female. This bias towards female sacrifices in elite burials reflects a similar bias seen thousands of years later, in the Eastern Zhou period of the early Iron Age (770–221 bc), in which grave owners were buried alongside sacrificed female companions5. Although it is interesting that the phenomena are similar, it is not clear whether they are connected.

Ancient DNA traces family lines and political shifts in the Avar empire![](http://media.nature.com/w400/magazine-assets/d41586-025-03593-5/d41586-025-03593-5_50467522.jpg)


Most of the sacrificed individuals in Shimao had similar genetic backgrounds to other people in the settlement, but two outliers were related to populations farther to the north or northwest. It should be noted that sacrificed individuals who are genetically similar to local people can still come from distant locations. Technologies such as isotopic analysis, which traces chemical signatures in skeletal remains to give hints about their geographical origin, could help to distinguish local from non-local people.

Chen and colleagues next looked at kinship practices in the Shimao population. They reported limited genetic diversity on the Y chromosome, especially among the elites, and found that men who were buried with human sacrifices, indicative of their elite status, were paternally related. This suggests that power and social status were inherited through the male line — a patrilineal social structure. By contrast, a study6 from June this year reported a late Neolithic community in eastern China (dating to 4,700–4,500 years ago) that was matrilineal, meaning inheritance was through the maternal line. It will be interesting to see whether spatial and temporal patterns emerge as more ancient-genomics studies of Neolithic communities in China are published.

The people of Shimao showed high genetic variability in the parts of the genome that are inherited exclusively from the maternal line, which reside in organelles called mitochondria. This means that women were probably incomers with diverse origins. Burials of female elites were also found at Shimao, but none of their close relatives was found. It is difficult to know why these women had a high social standing — was it because of their husbands, their maternal family or their own achievements?

A lot has been learnt about the complex population histories in prehistoric East Asia from ancient-DNA studies published in the past decade7–10, but there are still many gaps in sampling that prevent fine-scale interpretations. For instance, Shimao people are genetically similar to contemporary populations from Taosi, another impressive settlement located about 400 kilometres south of Shimao. But without information on pre-Taosi populations in that region, it’s not clear whether Shimao and Taosi only became similar during the late Longshan period, or if their preceding populations were already similar and they developed relatively independently but had continued interactions.

The northern steppe population is also severely under-represented in the ancient-DNA field in general — a single genome from the Yumin site (about 4,000 years older than Shimao) was used for comparisons in this study. Studying contemporary populations from the steppe region will greatly help to fine-tune interpretations about the link between Shimao and the northern steppe. Chen and colleagues provide an important peek into possible genetic connections, but further ancient-genomics studies are needed to reliably determine the genetic relationships between prehistoric populations.

title: Shape-shifting electrodes tune optical-frequency converter
content:
Tools that can perform several tasks are crucial for research, particularly in emerging fields, because they provide the flexibility to explore a problem without the need to build many types of prototype device. Writing in *Nature*, Yanagimoto *et al*.1 report an optical device that generates a spectrum of light with properties that can be adjusted *in situ* as needed. Their approach uses an optical process called second-harmonic generation, which doubles the frequency of light. The authors show that this process can be reprogrammed by projecting different patterns of light onto an electrode on the device’s surface.

Read the paper: Programmable on-chip nonlinear photonics![](http://media.nature.com/w400/magazine-assets/d41586-025-03452-3/d41586-025-03452-3_51758060.jpg)


In the field of electronics, reprogrammable circuits, which have been commercially available since the 1980s2, provide an efficient way to produce prototype devices. Field-programmable devices — which have functionality that can be adapted by the user — are also available in optics. An example is spatial light modulators, which are engineered surfaces that modify the properties of incident light in a spatially varying fashion, meaning that light will be modulated differently depending on where on the material’s surface it hits.

For more than a decade, researchers have been developing field-programmable photonic integrated circuits (PICs)3, which are microchips that process light rather than electronic currents. However, these programmable PICs have been engineered mostly for optical processes in which the response of the light to the medium through which it propagates is linearly proportional to the light’s intensity. Such processes cannot modify the frequency (colour) of light. Frequency conversion, which is required for many applications, must instead use ‘nonlinear’ optical processes.

One example of a nonlinear optical phenomenon is second-harmonic generation, in which the interaction between light and a material doubles the light’s frequency. Light has wave-like properties, so it can be described by periodic maxima and minima. When two light waves interact, the difference in the position of their maxima and minima is characterized by a quantity called the phase difference. Frequency-conversion processes, such as second-harmonic generation, typically require the phase difference between the input and output light waves to be fixed as the waves propagate through the material — a criterion called phase matching. Phase matching is difficult to achieve because the speed at which light travels through a material depends on its frequency. This effect, which is called dispersion, results in a phase difference between the input and output waves that accumulates as they propagate through the material, because the frequency of the output light is higher than that of the input light.

Light detectors made from perovskite crystals see in full colour![](http://media.nature.com/w400/magazine-assets/d41586-025-03452-3/d41586-025-03452-3_51758056.jpg)


To overcome dispersion, researchers often use a technique called quasi-phase-matching4, in which the phase difference is periodically reset. Quasi-phase-matching is usually implemented using a method called poling, in which periodically spaced regions of electric field in the device, created by patterning the surface with electrodes, cause a periodic change in the properties of the material. The accumulated phase difference is reversed each time the light travels through a modified region, so that, on average, the desired phase relationship between the two waves is achieved.

The separation between the electrodes determines the frequency of light that can undergo second-harmonic generation in the material. However, once a material has been poled, it cannot be reconfigured easily without the fabrication of new electrodes. Although many impressive demonstrations have been reported5, PICs that change the frequency of light have generally had static properties that are optimized for a single purpose.

Yanagimoto *et al*. built a reprogrammable, microscale device for second-harmonic generation (Fig. 1). The frequency-doubled light was generated in a tiny slab of silicon nitride a few micrometres thick. Structures such as this, which direct the propagation of light, are called waveguides. Silicon nitride is commonly used for waveguides, but it does not usually support the standard mechanism for second-harmonic generation. However, all materials can exhibit third-harmonic generation, in which light that interacts with the material triples in frequency. A direct current (DC) electric field (one that is steady in time) applied to a silicon nitride waveguide can convert the phenomenon that is responsible for third-harmonic generation into one that produces second-harmonic generation.

![Figure 1](http://media.nature.com/lw767/magazine-assets/d41586-025-03452-3/d41586-025-03452-3_51757992.jpg)

**Figure 1 | Reconfigurable frequency doubling of light.** Second-harmonic generation, which doubles the frequency of light through its interaction with a material, can be achieved by introducing periodic regions of time-invariant electric field into the material using patterned electrodes on its surface. Yanagimoto *et al*.1 report a method to modify the electrode pattern *in situ*. Laser light is directed through a silicon nitride ‘waveguide’ which is covered on one side by a uniform, transparent electrode. Between the electrode and the waveguide is a photoconductor (a material with electric conductivity that can be modified by light). Illuminating the photoconductor with an optical pattern results in that pattern being imprinted on the electric field in the waveguide. The output spectrum of light depends on the illumination pattern. In this figure, the period of the illumination pattern varies in the transverse direction. In regions in which the period is optimized to the frequency of the laser, an intensity peak of frequency-doubled light is output from the device.

The authors introduced an innovation that made their device programmable and reconfigurable. A single uniform and transparent electrode was deposited on the waveguide, and a fixed voltage was applied between the top and bottom of the device. On its own, this would generate a spatially uniform electric field in the waveguide. However, the researchers introduced, between the electrode and the waveguide, a layer of a type of material called a photoconductor, which has electric conductivity that can be modified using light. The electric field could reach the waveguide only in regions in which the photoconductor was illuminated. The illumination pattern could be easily varied and reprogrammed using a spatial light modulator.

The authors sent a laser through the waveguide and projected a striped illumination pattern onto it, in which the stripes were in the transverse direction, meaning they were perpendicular to the propagation direction of the laser. If the separation between the stripes — which is called the period of the illumination pattern — was optimized for quasi-phase matching, then second-harmonic generation occurred, doubling the frequency of the laser light.

The authors tested various illumination patterns in which the period of the illumination pattern varied along the direction of laser propagation (longitudinal direction). Depending on how this variation was introduced, the spectrum of the second-harmonic light could be tailored almost arbitrarily. This included cases in which the output intensity exhibited a sharp peak at a single frequency, sharp peaks at multiple frequencies or broadly distributed over a range of frequencies.

The authors also varied the illumination pattern in the transverse direction. This modified the spatial profile of the light, meaning that its intensity when it left the device varied at different points along the transverse direction. By modifying the striped illumination pattern in both the transverse and longitudinal directions, the authors engineered an output spectrum in which different frequencies of output light had different spatial profiles.

Moreover, the illumination pattern could be varied in time by updating the spatial light modulator. By characterizing the output light, the authors detected errors and environmental drifts and applied corrective feedback. This programmability might be invaluable for *in situ* inverse design, in which a desired output spectrum is realized by iteratively measuring the output and adjusting the illumination pattern accordingly.

Copper-free chips generate robust ‘combs’ of multicoloured light![](http://media.nature.com/w400/magazine-assets/d41586-025-03452-3/d41586-025-03452-3_51719300.jpg)


Although the work of Yanagimoto *et al*. showed unprecedented flexibility, the efficiency of the device was more than one million times smaller that of non-reprogrammable silicon-nitride-based PIC devices6. However, the authors show that this was mostly because of energy loss and reduced light intensity associated with their waveguide design and fabrication, and not a fundamental limitation of their approach to reconfigurable second-harmonic generation.

To improve efficiency, the authors tested their method using a waveguide that had the shape of a narrow channel rather than a flat slab. Using a device that had a simple striped illumination pattern, they improved the efficiency of creating second-harmonic light by a factor of 40 and approached the efficiency of previous waveguide demonstrations7. Nevertheless, the waveguide performance was still lower than in optimized PIC devices6,7. This was partly due to losses induced by the photoconductive material — reducing this effect will be one challenge going forwards.

The potential applications of this work include highly tunable lasers for the spectroscopic analysis of materials and reconfigurable sources of light for quantum-networking applications. As well as the performance improvements described above, the use of smaller spatial light modulators and associated optical components, such as active metasurfaces8, might reduce the size of the optical projector and enable the illumination pattern to be updated more quickly — a crucial step if these reconfigurable devices are to be deployed outside a laboratory.

title: Double whammy: drugs that inhibit kinase enzymes also speed up their disposal
content:
This is a summary of: Scholes, N. S. *et al*. Inhibitors supercharge kinase turnover through native proteolytic circuits. *Nature* https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09763-9 (2025).

## The mission

Using targeted ‘degrader’ drugs to promote the elimination of certain proteins is an established pharmacological strategy1. Degraders typically function by recruiting a target protein to a component of the cellular protein-disposal machinery that does not recognize the target in the degrader’s absence. However, many small molecules that were originally designed as conventional inhibitors can also trigger protein degradation2. This has frequently been reported for inhibitors of protein kinases, a family of enzymes that orchestrates cellular signalling. However, how, and how often, inhibition turns into degradation remains unclear. Does binding directly mark a target for destruction, or does it rewire signalling networks to expose hidden vulnerabilities in cellular quality-control circuits? Unless researchers can gain a quantitative and qualitative understanding of the underlying mechanisms, observations of this process will remain sporadic and unpredictable. Given that kinase inhibitors are a cornerstone of modern medicine, clarifying the molecular logic behind inhibitor-induced degradation is crucial to enable the process to be exploited for therapeutic benefit, and to anticipate any unwanted side effects when it is.

## The discovery

We built a bioluminescence platform that enables the abundance of kinases to be monitored in intact cells after treatment with various inhibitors. In total, we tested 1,570 inhibitors against 98 kinases, aiming to spot instances in which an inhibitor acted as a degrader. Our survey identified 232 compounds that reduced the abundance of at least one kinase (Fig. 1a). Many kinases require a chaperone protein, such as HSP90, to maintain their stability. We found that HSP90-stabilized kinases were particularly prone to induced degradation, consistent with the idea that inhibitors can disrupt the kinase–HSP90 interaction and trigger destabilization. However, many degradation events could not be explained by this phenomenon.

![Figure 1.](http://media.nature.com/lw767/magazine-assets/d41586-025-03816-9/d41586-025-03816-9_51757162.jpg)

**Figure 1 | Scalable discovery of inhibitor-induced degradation of kinase enzymes.** Kinases tagged with a luminescent reporter were expressed in a cell line to enable their abundance to be measured over time after treatment with kinase inhibitors. **a**, Heat map of inhibitors that elicit statistically significant degradation of one (pink) or multiple (teal) kinases, sorted according to observed degradation frequencies across kinases and compounds. Histograms show summed scores in both dimensions. **b**, Temporal screening trajectories of three selected hit compounds. Data show normalized change in kinase abundances, with mean (black lines) and confidence intervals (shading). Hit kinases (LYN, BLK and RIPK2, degraded by SRC inhibitor 3 (SI-3), TAK285 and RIPK-IN-4 (RI-4), respectively) are shown in pink. Detailed analyses of their mechanisms of action showed that natural degradation routes were accelerated in all three examples. POC, per cent over control.Credit: Scholes, N. S. *et al*./*Nature *(CC BY 4.0)

Mechanistic investigation of three representative cases (Fig. 1b) revealed a unifying concept in which inhibitors induce kinases to adopt a state in which they are more likely to be turned over by natural degradation mechanisms. In this way, kinase degradation is ‘supercharged’ through evolutionarily optimized cellular mechanisms. We identified a range of cues that prompt this accelerated degradation, including changes in the activity of the kinase, its cellular localization and how its individual molecules associate to form multimers.

## The implications

Our findings broaden the scope of small-molecule pharmacology. Instead of relying on engineered degrader modalities that physically link a protein to parts of the cellular degradation system, researchers might be able to use conventional inhibitors to exploit existing cellular clearance systems. By revealing how small molecules can reshape protein states and their recognition by natural quality-control machinery, this work introduces an alternative route that could be used to eliminate disease-relevant targets.

Our analysis covered only a fraction of the full set of kinases, and was performed in a single cell line derived from a type of blood cancer. The data therefore probably capture only the tip of the iceberg, and many kinases, contexts and protein families have yet to be investigated. Notably, related work3 involving our group shows that the same supercharging concept enables the degradation of non-kinase proteins, such as indoleamine-2,3-dioxygenase 1 (IDO1), which suggests that the principles presented here can be applied more broadly to other cellular proteins. Likewise, small molecules that induce the degradation of the oestrogen receptor in treatments for breast cancer have been shown to accelerate natural degradation pathways that coordinate the turnover of oestrogen-receptor molecules after they are bound by their natural ligand, oestradiol4.

Collectively, these findings demonstrate the potential wide-ranging applications of supercharging intrinsic degradation mechanisms. Future efforts should aim to map natural pathways of protein turnover more broadly and dissect how mutations — for example, those associated with cancer — might alter the activity of these routes. Understanding whether disease-driving variants are accessible to distinct, drug-tunable degradation mechanisms could thus open avenues for selective therapeutic intervention. — Natalie S. Scholes is at the CeMM, Research Center for Molecular Medicine, Vienna, Austria, and Georg E. Winter is at the AITHYRA Research Institute for Biomedical Artificial Intelligence, Vienna, Austria.

## Behind the paper

From the beginning of the project, we wanted to systematically explore both protein space and chemical space. This came with challenges. First, we needed a scalable way to monitor kinase abundance over time. After several attempts, we settled on luminescent reporters, and generated and screened 100 cell lines. The next challenge was to computationally dissect perturbations of individual kinases from ‘global’ perturbations across many kinases. Finally, we discovered some unexpected mechanisms. One highlight was our finding that the enzyme γ-secretase is a key mediator that enables kinase degradation. Published evidence suggested that it cleaves only proteins that span the cell membrane, and our target kinase was membrane-tethered. However, consistent with a previous study5, we showed that the membrane anchor is cleaved by γ-secretase, meaning that this mechanism could affect a broader spectrum of targets. Throughout the project, we had an incredible international team of collaborators, who supported us throughout the project. **— N.S.S.**

title: This AI combo could unlock human-level intelligence
content:
Will computers ever match or surpass human-level intelligence — and, if so, how? When the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AAAI), based in Washington DC, asked its members earlier this year whether neural networks — the current star of artificial-intelligence systems — alone will be enough to hit this goal, the vast majority said no. Instead, most said, a heavy dose of an older kind of AI will be needed to get these systems up to par: symbolic AI.

Will AI ever win its own Nobel? Some predict a prize-worthy science discovery soon![](http://media.nature.com/w400/magazine-assets/d41586-025-03856-1/d41586-025-03856-1_51539516.png)


Sometimes called ‘good old-fashioned AI’, symbolic AI is based on formal rules and an encoding of the logical relationships between concepts1. Mathematics is symbolic, for example, as are ‘if–then’ statements and computer coding languages such as Python, along with flow charts or Venn diagrams that map how, say, cats, mammals and animals are conceptually related. Decades ago, symbolic systems were an early front-runner in the AI effort. However, in the early 2010s, they were vastly outpaced by more-flexible neural networks. These machine-learning models excel at learning from vast amounts of data, and underlie large language models (LLMs), as well as chatbots such as ChatGPT.

Now, however, the computer-science community is pushing hard for a better and bolder melding of the old and the new. ‘Neurosymbolic AI’ has become the hottest buzzword in town. Brandon Colelough, a computer scientist at the University of Maryland in College Park, has charted the meteoric rise of the concept in academic papers (see ‘Going up and up’). These reveal a spike of interest in neurosymbolic AI that started in around 2021 and shows no sign of slowing down2.

Plenty of researchers are heralding the trend as an escape from what they see as an unhealthy monopoly of neural networks in AI research, and expect the shift to deliver smarter and more reliable AI.

A better melding of these two strategies could lead to artificial general intelligence (AGI): AI that can reason and generalize its knowledge from one situation to another as well as humans do. It might also be useful for high-risk applications, such as military or medical decision-making, says Colelough. Because symbolic AI is transparent and understandable to humans, he says, it doesn’t suffer from the ‘black box’ syndrome that can make neural networks hard to trust.

![GOING UP AND UP: bar chart showing the increase in published papers on neurosymbolic AI between 1995 to 2024. The past five years show an increase from fewer than 10 to more than 200 per year.](http://media.nature.com/lw767/magazine-assets/d41586-025-03856-1/d41586-025-03856-1_51751370.jpg)

Source: updated from ref. 2

There are already good examples of neurosymbolic AI, including Google DeepMind’s AlphaGeometry, a system reported last year3 that can reliably solve maths Olympiad problems — questions aimed at talented secondary-school students. But working out how best to combine neural networks and symbolic AI into an all-purpose system is a formidable challenge.

“You’re really architecting this kind of two-headed beast,” says computer scientist William Regli, also at the University of Maryland.

## War of words

In 2019, computer scientist Richard Sutton posted a short essay entitled ‘The bitter lesson’ on his blog (see go.nature.com/4paxykf). In it, he argued that, since the 1950s, people have repeatedly assumed that the best way to make intelligent computers is to feed them with all the insights that humans have arrived at about the rules of the world, in fields from physics to social behaviour. The bitter pill to swallow, wrote Sutton, is that time and time again, symbolic methods have been outdone by systems that use a ton of raw data and scaled-up computational power to leverage ‘search and learning’. Early chess-playing computers, for example, that were trained on human-devised strategies were outperformed by those that were simply fed lots of game data.

This lesson has been widely quoted by proponents of neural networks to support the idea that making these systems ever-bigger is the best path to AGI. But many researchers argue that the essay overstates its case and downplays the crucial part that symbolic systems can and do play in AI. For example, the best chess program today, *Stockfish*, pairs a neural network with a symbolic tree of allowable moves.

AI models that lie, cheat and plot murder: how dangerous are LLMs really?![](http://media.nature.com/w400/magazine-assets/d41586-025-03856-1/d41586-025-03856-1_51740964.jpg)


Neural nets and symbolic algorithms both have pros and cons. Neural networks are made up of layers of nodes with weighted connections that are adjusted during training to recognize patterns and learn from data. They are fast and creative, but they are also bound to make things up and can’t reliably answer questions beyond the scope of their training data.

Symbolic systems, meanwhile, struggle to encompass ‘messy’ concepts, such as human language, that involve vast rule databases that are difficult to build and slow to search. But their workings are clear, and they are good at reasoning, using logic to apply their general knowledge to fresh situations.

When put to use in the real world, neural networks that lack symbolic knowledge make classic mistakes: image generators might draw people with six fingers on each hand because they haven’t learnt the general concept that hands typically have five; video generators struggle to make a ball bounce around a scene because they haven’t learnt that gravity pulls things downwards. Some researchers blame such mistakes on a lack of data or computing power, but others say that the mistakes illustrate neural networks’ fundamental inability to generalize knowledge and reason logically.

Many argue that adding symbolism to neural nets might be the best — even the only — way to inject logical reasoning into AI. The global technology firm IBM, for example, is backing neurosymbolic techniques as a path to AGI. But others remain sceptical: Yann LeCun, one of the fathers of modern AI and chief AI scientist at tech giant Meta, has said that neurosymbolic approaches are “incompatible” with neural-network learning.

Sutton, who is at the University of Alberta in Edmonton, Canada, and won the 2024 Turing prize, the equivalent of the Nobel prize for computer science, holds firm to his original argument: “The bitter lesson still applies to today’s AI,” he told *Nature*. This suggests, he says, that “adding a symbolic, more manually crafted element is probably a mistake”.

Gary Marcus, an AI entrepreneur, writer and cognitive scientist based in Vancouver, Canada, and one of the most vocal advocates of neurosymbolic AI, tends to frame this difference of opinions as a philosophical battle that is now being settled in his favour.

Others, such as roboticist Leslie Kaelbling at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge, say that arguments over which view is right are a distraction, and that people should just get on with whatever works. “I’m a magpie. I’ll do anything that makes my robots better.”

## Mix and match

Beyond the fact that neurosymbolic AI aims to meld the benefits of neural nets with the benefits of symbolism, its definition is blurry. Neurosymbolic AI encompasses “a very large universe”, says Marcus, “of which we’ve explored only a tiny bit”.

There are many broad approaches, which people have attempted to categorize in various ways. One option highlighted by many is the use of symbolic techniques to improve neural nets4. AlphaGeometry is arguably one of the most sophisticated examples of this strategy: it trains a neural net on a synthetic data set of maths problems produced using a symbolic computer language, making the solutions easier to check and ensuring fewer mistakes. It combines the two elegantly, says Colelough. In another example, ‘logic tensor networks’ provide a way to encode symbolic logic for neural networks. Statements can be assigned a fuzzy-truth value5: a number somewhere between 1 (true) and 0 (false). This provides a framework of rules to help the system reason.

Another broad approach does what some would say is the reverse, using neural nets to finesse symbolic algorithms. One problem with symbolic knowledge databases is that they are often so large that they take a very long time to search: the ‘tree’ of all possible moves in a game of Go, for example, contains about 10170 positions, which is unfeasibly large to crunch through. Neural networks can be trained to predict the most promising subset of moves, allowing the system to cut down how much of the ‘tree’ it has to search, and thus speeding up the time it takes to settle on the best move. That’s what Google’s AlphaGo did when it famously outperformed a Go grandmaster.

AI ‘scientists’ joined these research teams: here’s what happened![](http://media.nature.com/w400/magazine-assets/d41586-025-03856-1/d41586-025-03856-1_51349070.jpg)


An alternative idea is to insert symbolics into the middle of an LLM’s workflow, in the same way as consulting a calculator might help person to solve a maths puzzle. Using rules-based systems during crucial reasoning steps can help to keep LLMs from going off-track, many argue. Projects including the Program-Aided Language (PAL) model, for example, use an LLM to convert natural-language tasks into Python code, use that symbolic code to solve the problem, and then interpret that solution back into natural language with an LLM6.

Jiayuan Mao, an AI researcher who has just completed her PhD at MIT with Kaelbling and is on her way to the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, has had success in using neurosymbolic AI to make robot training more efficient. Her strategy is to use a neural network to recognize objects (such as a red rubber ball or a green glass cube) in a visual field and then use a symbolic algorithm to reason through relational questions about those objects (such as ‘is the rubber object behind the green object?’). A pure neural network would need 700,000 examples in its training data to achieve 99% accuracy on this task, she says. But by adding symbolic techniques, she needs just 10% of that number7. “Even if you use 1%, you can still get 92% accuracy, which is quite impressive,” she says. A similar neurosymbolic system she created trounced a neural-network-based system at guiding a robot that encountered unfamiliar objects while washing dishes or making tea8.

## Lost in translation

One of the big challenges for symbolic AI is how to encode sometimes slippery human knowledge within a language of logic and rules. One of the earliest attempts was a project called Cyc, started by computer scientist Doug Lenat in 1984 and later overseen by his AI company Cycorp, based in Austin, Texas. The intent was to explicitly articulate common-sense facts and rules of thumb, such as ‘a daughter is a child’, ‘people love their children’ and ‘seeing someone you love makes you smile’. The project’s language, CycL, uses symbols (for logical operators such as IF, AND, OR and NOT) to express logical relationships so that an inference engine can easily draw conclusions, such as ‘seeing your child would make you smile’.

Cyc, which now holds more than 25 million axioms, has been used in a variety of AI efforts and has inspired other projects, such as Google’s Knowledge Graph, which holds more than 500 billion facts. Today, ‘knowledge engineers’ use a similar strategy to gather human-generated facts and relationships, build specialized databases and integrate them with AI.

Symbolic databases can help an AI to generalize knowledge from one situation and apply it in another, says Kaelbling, which is a powerful way to make reasoning more efficient. But there is a trade-off in accuracy when dealing with subjects for which there are many exceptions to the ‘rules’ — not all people love their children, for example, and seeing something you love doesn’t always make you smile. Symbolics should be incorporated only when it is helpful to do so, she says. “Cyc was trying to turn common sense into math. That is almost surely a bad idea,” Kaelbling says.

Universities are embracing AI: will students get smarter or stop thinking?![](http://media.nature.com/w400/magazine-assets/d41586-025-03856-1/d41586-025-03856-1_51676284.jpg)


In 2023, Marcus posted a paper9 with Lenat laying out what LLMs can learn from Cyc. As part of that work, the duo asked GPT-3, an early LLM of the type that underpins ChatGPT, to write CycL statements that encode the logical relationships in the sentence “Did you touch a blue object located in the capital of France on September 25th, 2022?” The response “at first amazed the Cyc team”, they report, because it generated what looked to be the right sort of statements in the right sort of language. But on closer inspection, GPT-3 made many crucial errors, they write, such as concluding that “the thing that is touching the blue object is the date”.

“It looks like it’s good, it looks like it should work, but it’s absolutely garbage,” says Colelough. This shows that it’s pointless to simply ram together a symbolic engine and a neural net, he says. “Then you might as well just not have the neurosymbolic system.”

What’s needed, Colelough says, is a lot more research on AI ‘metacognition’ — how AI monitors and conducts its own thinking. That would enable AI ‘conductors’ to oversee a more sophisticated integration of the two paradigms, rather than having different engines simply take turns. Colelough says AlphaGeometry does this well, but in a limited context. If a flexible conductor that works for any domain of knowledge could be developed, “that would be AGI for me”, Colelough says.

There’s a lot more work to do. Fresh hardware and chip architectures might be needed to run neurosymbolic AI efficiently10. In time, other types of AI — maybe based on neural networks, symbolic AI, both or neither — might become more exciting, such as quantum AI, a fledgling field that seeks to exploit the properties of the quantum world to improve AI.

For Mao, the ultimate goal is to leverage neural networks’ learning abilities to create rules, categories and paths of reasoning that humans aren’t yet aware of. “The hope is that eventually we can have systems that also invent their own symbolic representation and symbolic algorithms, so that they can really go beyond what a human knows,” she says. That might be like a computer discovering an as-yet-unknown mathematical or physical concept — perhaps analogous to π or the property of mass — and then encoding the new concept to help to extend knowledge. “We need to study how computers can teach humans, not how humans can teach machines.”

title: Chile must preserve international science in Antarctica
content:
For decades, Chile has helped scientists from across the world to study Antarctica, providing logistical support and rescue services from its southernmost region. But this role is under threat. These services are supported by annual short-term government funding. The two candidates who reached the second round of the ongoing presidential election have put little emphasis on Antarctica, suggesting a worrying lack of interest.

The government should take heed of the recent ‘Mesa Antártica’ consensus document (go.nature.com/3xmm3cd; in Spanish), produced by more than 40 Chilean Antarctic researchers and experts, including us, as part of a national initiative that seeks to develop a road map for Chile’s future. It recommends modernizing the country’s Antarctic governance model by creating a coordinated authority for logistics, science and diplomacy; ensuring multi-year funding for long-term observation systems; and deepening international scientific partnerships using Chilean infrastructure as a shared platform.

These changes would enable partner nations to plan joint field campaigns, interoperable logistics and long-term environmental monitoring, and allow Chile to continue its historic service to the international community.

title: Trump’s AI ‘Genesis Mission’: what are the risks and opportunities?
content:
![Close up of a microchip on a computer circuit board decorated with the flag of United States of America.](http://media.nature.com/lw767/magazine-assets/d41586-025-03890-z/d41586-025-03890-z_51762452.jpg)

The Genesis Mission aims to provide researchers with the computing power and data sets necessary to train artificial-intelligence models.Credit: William Potter/iStock via Getty

The White House has launched a plan to accelerate research in the United States, by building artificial intelligence (AI) models on the rich scientific data sets held by the country’s 17 national laboratories, as well as harnessing their enormous computing resources.

An executive order issued on 24 November instructs the US Department of Energy (DoE) to create a platform through which academic researchers and AI firms can create powerful AI models using the government’s scientific data. Framed as part of a race for global technology dominance, it lists collaborations with technology firms including Microsoft, IBM, OpenAI, Google and Anthropic, as well as quantum-computing companies such as Quantinuum. Such a vast public–private partnership would give companies unprecedented access to federal scientific data sets for AI-driven analysis.

The effort, dubbed the Genesis Mission, aims to “double the productivity and impact of American research and innovation within a decade”, in a variety of fields from fusion energy to medicine. The project expects to “unlock breakthroughs in medicine, energy, materials science and beyond”, says Michael Kratsios, the US president’s science adviser. It also aims to build AI agents — general models with the ability to harness tools such as specialized software and coding suites — that can generate hypotheses and automate research workflows.

Labs around the world are already training AI systems on scientific data, to boost their capabilities in scientific domains and attempting to use AI models to make discoveries. But some researchers remain sceptical that general AI tools are capable of making truly fresh insights, and warn that their inherent flaws make the value of agents unclear.

The new US initiative formalizes and expands ongoing AI research efforts by the administration of President Donald Trump. “The impact is that it enables many more scientists and researchers to have access to all of the infrastructure that they need to explore important scientific questions that the country cares about,” says Lynne Parker, a robotics engineer at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, who led AI-policy initiatives for the administrations of Trump and his predecessor, Joe Biden, but was not involved in the current initiative. “That really has not been possible before.”

![An aerial view of the many buildings of the Argonne National Laboratory campus in Illinois.](http://media.nature.com/lw767/magazine-assets/d41586-025-03890-z/d41586-025-03890-z_51762450.jpg)

Supercomputers at national laboratories, including the Argonne National Laboratory in Illinois, will probably be used as part of the Genesis Mission.Credit: Argonne National Laboratory/Getty

Trump’s team has been working to funnel money and attention to AI projects even as it tries to gut federal research spending more broadly. The White House has the power to shape the direction of research at the DoE’s network of national laboratories. It did not give an estimated price tag for the AI initiative; any extra funding beyond the laboratories’ normal budgets would have to be approved by the US Congress.

*Nature *looks at how the project might affect researchers and AI companies, and its promises and risks.

## What are government-funded scientists being asked to do?

The scale and timeline of the plan is ambitious. In 60 days, the DoE is expected to create a list of 20 potential science and technology challenges for the project to tackle, in areas of national priorities such as nuclear fusion, quantum information science and crucial materials. The agency is supposed to create a full inventory of available federal computing resources and identify initial data assets to use, then work out how to safely include external data sets. The administration expects to demonstrate the platform’s capability for one of these research challenges in nine months.

These early steps will probably build on projects that are already under way at the national laboratories. For instance, Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee has been working on advancing AI research using a hybrid approach that uses both quantum and classical computing. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in California is using AI to find ways to speed up network traffic.

How AI agents will change research: a scientist’s guide![](http://media.nature.com/w400/magazine-assets/d41586-025-03890-z/d41586-025-03890-z_51572570.png)


The “DoE has been making a case for ‘AI for science’ for over seven years, and this executive order is the starting pistol to get on with it”, says Michael Norman, an astrophysicist at the University of California, San Diego, and former director of the San Diego Supercomputer Center. “It is an exciting direction indeed.”

## What are companies being asked to do?

The project has named more than 50 collaborating companies, including some that have already been working on their own ‘AI scientists’. FutureHouse, a start-up based in San Francisco, California, for instance, launched a commercially available, AI-driven research platform earlier this month.

The precise role of these private companies in the Genesis plan remains unclear — although Trump’s executive order says the project will entail “collaboration with external partners possessing advanced AI, data, or computing capabilities or scientific domain expertise”. Such partnerships could include research agreements to jointly develop technologies, or a user-facility agreement for external researchers to conduct work in government facilities. Chip-manufacturing and computer companies such as NVIDIA, Advanced Micro Devices and Hewlett Packard Enterprise have reportedly agreed to build facilities in national labs, according to a report by *The New York Times*.

Three ways ex-CDC chief says that Trump team is sidelining science![](http://media.nature.com/w400/magazine-assets/d41586-025-03890-z/d41586-025-03890-z_51459098.jpg)


Some partnerships are already under way. In October, for instance, Argonne National Laboratory in Illinois announced a partnership with NVIDIA and technology firm Oracle to build two next-generation AI supercomputing systems. At least two national laboratories already have arrangements with the company OpenAI, based in San Francisco, California, to host local AI models that can process classified data on computers in the facilities. In February, the company held an ‘AI jam session’ with researchers from nine US national labs that allowed scientists to test the use of OpenAI’s reasoning models in their specific domains.

## What are the opportunities?

The new Genesis Mission is meant to provide “secure access to appropriate datasets, including proprietary, federally curated, and open scientific datasets, in addition to synthetic data generated through DOE computing resources”, according to the executive order. Creating a national-scale platform that harnesses rich data sets usually housed in the walls of the national laboratories could be a boon for researchers. Although task-specific models such as the protein-folding model AlphaFold were built on open scientific data sets, general-purpose AI systems such as OpenAI’s GPT-5 are thought to be largely built on data scraped from the Internet.

It isn’t yet clear which data sets would be involved, but possible candidates include information gathered at facilities such as the Spallation Neutron Source at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. That facility collects neutron-scattering data, which illuminate how materials behave at the atomic scale, says Georgia Tourassi, the lab's associate director for computing and computational sciences. “From atomistic measurements to exascale simulations, such data sets can immediately accelerate the development of trustworthy, science-capable AI models,” she says.

Beyond AlphaFold: how AI is decoding the grammar of the genome![](http://media.nature.com/w400/magazine-assets/d41586-025-03890-z/d41586-025-03890-z_51556680.png)


Access to the DoE’s computing power could also accelerate research. Argonne’s Aurora supercomputer, for example, uses graphics processing units, known as GPUs, that make it particularly suitable for AI, which requires huge parallel processing power.

## What are the risks and challenges?

For starters, Congress might not allocate enough money to the DoE to achieve its ambitious plans, which the Trump administration compares “in urgency and ambition” with the Manhattan Project, the secret multi-billion-dollar US government programme that produced the first nuclear weapons. Trump has proposed cutting the DoE’s science budget by 14% for the 2026 fiscal year and funding for AI might entail drawing funds from elsewhere in the budget.

Data security is another big question. Trump’s executive order says all data will be handled consistently with regard to law, classification, privacy and intellectual property protections. Tourassi says she expects data to be made available “in alignment with the established data-sharing policies of our user facilities and sponsor programmes”.

Then there’s the issue of how to wrangle all these disparate data sets into a single user-friendly platform. “Transforming isolated datasets into a unified engine for discovery” will be a major challenge, wrote Darío Gil, the DoE under-secretary for science who will head the project, and physicist Kathryn Moler at Stanford University in California, in an editorial in *Science*. They note that some of the most successful big-science projects in recent years, such as the Protein Data Bank repository and the Large Hadron Collider particle accelerator at CERN, Europe’s particle-physics laboratory near Geneva, Switzerland, succeeded because they were open source and relied on well-structured data — which is not always the case with large data sets.

Parker says she would have liked to have seen more in the Genesis Mission plans about how more US scientists could participate in this research. As it stands, most of the benefit might flow to researchers who already work with DoE-funded platforms.

The plan is also forging ahead without any comprehensive federal legislation to regulate AI. In January, Trump revoked an executive order that was created by Biden aimed at ensuring AI safety. The Trump administration has positioned itself pro-industry and called for federal funding for AI to be withheld from any state with “burdensome AI regulations”.

Many researchers argue that AI applied to science can benefit humanity. But they say that companies pursuing intelligence with broad capabilities, beyond those of humans, and without strict safety guard-rails or limits on AI power, bring a range of risks.

“The Genesis Mission will succeed if it enables America’s best scientists to leverage specialized AI for science, and fail if it becomes a mere subsidy for private companies building superintelligent AI that threatens national and global security,” says Andrea Miotti, founder of ControlAI, a London-based non-profit organization that works to reduce the risks to humanity from artificial intelligence.

title: Polyclonal origins of human premalignant colorectal lesions
content:
## Abstract

Cancer is generally thought to be caused by expansion of a single mutant cell1. However, analyses of early colorectal cancer lesions suggest that tumors may instead originate from multiple, genetically distinct cell populations2,3. Detecting polyclonal tumor initiation is challenging in patients, as it requires profiling early-stage lesions before clonal sweeps obscure diversity. To investigate this, we analyzed normal colorectal mucosa, benign and dysplastic premalignant polyps, and malignant adenocarcinomas (123 samples) from six individuals with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP). Individuals with FAP have a germline heterozygous *APC* mutation, predisposing them to colorectal cancer and numerous premalignant polyps by early adulthood4. Whole-genome and/or whole-exome sequencing revealed that many premalignant polyps—40% with benign histology and 28% with dysplasia—were composed of multiple genetic lineages that diverged early, consistent with polyclonal origins. This conclusion was reinforced by whole-genome sequencing of single crypts from multiple polyps in additional patients which showed limited sharing of mutations among crypts within the same lesion. In some cases, multiple distinct *APC* mutations co-existed in different lineages of a single polyp, consistent with polyclonality. These findings reshape our understanding of early neoplastic events, demonstrating that tumor initiation can arise from the convergence of diverse mutant clones. They also suggest that cell-intrinsic growth advantages alone may not fully explain tumor initiation, highlighting the importance of microenvironmental and tissue-level factors in early cancer evolution.
